stops.name: Lancaster, the architect's second son
stops.date_confidence: attested (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; Britannica; Wikipedia). One source in the pool, encyclopedia.com, gives 28 March instead; the discrepancy is recorded, not resolved. The father's occupation is corrected here: he was an architect first and became a school secretary in 1921, not a schoolmaster who turned architect.
stops.campa: John Langshaw Austin is born on the twenty-sixth of March 1911, second son of Geoffrey Langshaw Austin, an architect, and Mary Hutton Bowes-Wilson. Lancaster is a mill and market town on the Lune, wool and oilcloth, its port silted up a century back. The Norman castle above the river is still in service as the county assize court, a room where what changes a man's life is a sentence spoken aloud by someone entitled to speak it. The family is gone from Lancashire before Austin turns eleven. No biography names the street or the house, and the town-centre pin is as close as the record comes.
suggested_refs: Lancaster Castle, in use as the county assize court throughout Austin's childhood
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'John Langshaw Austin'
Britannica, 'J.L. Austin'
Wikipedia, 'J. L. Austin'

stops.name: St Andrews, the school secretary's household
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Wikipedia; HandWiki); month and day unknown and defaulted to 01. Coordinate corrected: the pool carried 56.3315/-2.794, about 860 m south of St Leonards School, past the harbour toward Kinkell Braes. Wikipedia's infobox for the school gives 56.3390/-2.7904.
stops.campa: The family leaves Lancashire for Fife, where Geoffrey Austin takes the post of secretary to St Leonards School, a girls' boarding school on the coast. John is ten. St Andrews is grey stone and sea wind, a university town built around a ruined cathedral and the shell of a castle on the rocks. The household income now comes out of an institution rather than a private architectural practice, and the boy's home address is a school he does not attend. At thirteen he will be sent south to Shrewsbury, and after that St Leonards is chiefly where the holiday letters reach him.
suggested_refs: St Leonards School, St Andrews, where Geoffrey Langshaw Austin served as secretary from 1921
sources: Wikipedia, 'J. L. Austin'

stops.name: Shrewsbury School, the Classics scholarship
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Wikipedia; Britannica); month and day defaulted to 01. Coordinate corrected: the pool gave 52.7075/-2.7602, about 430 m off. Shrewsbury School has stood on the Kingsland site, south bank of the Severn, since 1882, at 52.7038/-2.7622.
stops.campa: At thirteen he wins a scholarship in Classics to Shrewsbury School, on its bluff above a bend of the Severn. Shrewsbury runs boys through Greek and Latin composition with the seriousness of a seminary: an English sentence goes in, and what comes out has to be idiomatic in a language nobody has spoken for two thousand years. Austin is unremarkable in most subjects and exact and fast in this one. He is here five years and leaves in 1929 a classicist. The work rewards a boy who reads closer than the paraphrase and notices the word a translation quietly drops.
suggested_refs: The Kingsland site of Shrewsbury School, occupied since 1882
sources: Britannica, 'J.L. Austin'
Wikipedia, 'J. L. Austin'

stops.name: Balliol College, Oxford, going up to read Greats
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Wikipedia; Britannica); the Michaelmas matriculation date is not given in the pool and the month and day default to 01. Coordinate corrected: the pool's 51.7548/-1.2544 sits about 230 m east of Balliol, on the Sheldonian and Clarendon Building block.
stops.campa: Austin goes up to Balliol to read Literae Humaniores, the four-year course pairing classical languages with ancient history and philosophy. Balliol in 1929 is the most self-consciously serious college in Oxford, proud of the viceroys and permanent secretaries it turns out, and Greats is built to produce exactly that mind: one trained to move between a Greek verb form and a question in ethics without noticing the seam. The philosophy comes in the second half of the course. For now it is Thucydides and syntax, and within a year he takes a First in Classical Moderations.

sources: Britannica, 'J.L. Austin'

stops.name: Sheldonian Theatre, Oxford, the Gaisford Prize
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The prize and its year are attested (Wikipedia; Britannica), but the Sheldonian as the venue is convention for Oxford prize ceremony and is not documented for this particular award. Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: He wins the Gaisford Prize for Greek Prose at twenty, one of Oxford's oldest classical competitions, judged on an unseen English passage turned into idiomatic ancient Greek. Prizes of this kind are announced under Wren's painted ceiling in the Sheldonian, the hall the university put up for exactly this sort of ceremony. It is a narrow technical honour, worth nothing outside Oxford and a good deal inside it, and what it certifies is a hand for the exact word in a dead language. Two years of Greats are still to sit.
suggested_refs: The Gaisford Prize for Greek Prose, founded 1855
sources: Wikipedia, 'J. L. Austin'

stops.name: Examination Schools, Oxford, the First in Greats
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Britannica; Wikipedia); Trinity term is the standard sitting for Final Honour Schools and the month is inferred, the day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Four years of Greek, Latin, ancient history and philosophy come down to a run of three-hour papers in the building the university raised in the 1880s expressly to house its exam season, the long corridors and numbered rooms still working exactly as designed. Greats examines the languages, the ancient historians and the philosophy together, on the assumption that a man who can construe Thucydides can be trusted with Aristotle. Austin is twenty-two. He takes a First.
suggested_refs: The Examination Schools, High Street, Oxford, opened 1882
sources: Britannica, 'J.L. Austin'

stops.name: All Souls College, Oxford, the prize fellowship
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Wikipedia; Nagel, 'Leader of the Martians', LRB). The election is conventionally held in the Michaelmas term and the month is inferred; the day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: Later the same year Austin sits the All Souls Prize Fellowship examination and is elected. The college has no undergraduates at all: it is built to hold Fellows, a library, and twin sundial towers on the High Street, and its examination is famous for questions with no correct answer, set to watch how a mind moves rather than to check what it already knows. At twenty-two he is funded to read with no teaching attached to the money. He spends these years deep in Aristotle.
suggested_refs: The All Souls Prize Fellowship examination, and its reputation for unanswerable questions
sources: Wikipedia, 'J. L. Austin'

stops.name: Magdalen College, Oxford, fellow and tutor in philosophy
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Britannica; Wikipedia; Rowe); month and day defaulted to 01. Coordinate reconciled: the pool carried two different and both incorrect pins for Magdalen, 51.7519/-1.2419 in the geography lens, which lands in the deer park east of the college, and 51.7526/-1.2494 in the afterlife lens, which lands nearer the Examination Schools. Wikipedia gives 51.7524/-1.2471.
stops.campa: Austin moves from All Souls to Magdalen as Fellow and Tutor in Philosophy, trading a fellowship built for pure research for one that comes with undergraduates, a deer park, and a bell tower sung from at dawn on May Morning. He now has to teach: Aristotle's ethics and logic, Leibniz, the standard Greats syllabus, week after week, to pupils who will mostly forget it. He does this for five years, an hour at a time. In a tutorial the argument is said out loud, across a table, to somebody who is permitted to answer that he does not see it.

stops.name: All Souls College, Oxford, the group that took Ayer apart
stops.date_confidence: the weekly group is attested for roughly 1936 to 1939 (Nagel, LRB, following Rowe); no start date, and month and day default to 01. The exact rooms are not specified in any source consulted, and All Souls stands here as the setting the sources associate with the group through Berlin's own fellowship. Membership corrected: the pool named only Berlin and Ayer, and Stuart Hampshire is a core member.
stops.campa: From about 1936 Austin runs a weekly discussion group of young dons, Isaiah Berlin, A. J. Ayer and Stuart Hampshire among them, meeting to take Ayer's logical positivism apart sentence by sentence. Where Ayer wants a verification principle to sort sense from nonsense once and for all, Austin keeps returning to a smaller question the positivists have no place for: what a person is actually doing with this sentence, on this occasion, in front of these people. Berlin will later call him the sharpest close reader of an argument he ever watched work. The group breaks up in 1939.
suggested_refs: A. J. Ayer, Language, Truth and Logic (1936), the book the group met to dismantle
sources: Thomas Nagel, 'Leader of the Martians', London Review of Books vol. 45 no. 17

stops.name: Cambridge, the Moral Sciences Club and the meaning of a word
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested (Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy; Harris and Unnsteinsson, 'Wittgenstein's influence on Austin's philosophy of language'); the day is not recorded and defaults to 01. The room within Cambridge is not specified and the pin is the city centre.
stops.campa: Austin travels to Cambridge to read a paper, 'The Meaning of a Word,' to the Moral Sciences Club, the room-culture that had incubated Moore and Wittgenstein. The paper takes on the Blue Book directly and argues against any tidy general theory of meaning: words mean nothing apart from the particular occasions of their use. He builds deliberately strange invented sentences to find the point where ordinary usage gives way, and reads the paper again soon after to Oxford's own Jowett Society. The paper stays unpublished for twenty-one years, until Urmson and Warnock collect it. In July he is called up.
suggested_refs: Ludwig Wittgenstein, The Blue Book, dictated 1933-34, the target of Austin's paper
sources: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Austin, John Langshaw'
Daniel Harris and Elmar Unnsteinsson, 'Wittgenstein's influence on Austin's philosophy of language'

stops.name: Storey's Gate, Westminster, reporting to GHQ Home Forces
stops.date_confidence: attested (Nagel, LRB, summarising Rowe). The pool's chronology lens dates the call-up to July 1940 and the arrival at GHQ to 1 January 1941; both stand, and only the second is pinned.
stops.campa: On the first day of 1941 Austin reports to General Headquarters Home Forces at Storey's Gate, off St James's Park, a few hundred yards from the Cabinet War Rooms and on no shared chain of command with them. He is twenty-nine, and will not take a tutorial again for six years. He has spent the 1930s asking what a person is doing when they say a given sentence. The army wants sentences about what the German army is doing, written so that a general can act on them without reading further.

stops.name: Somerville College, Oxford, the marriage to Jean Coutts
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested (Wikipedia; Grokipedia, 'Jean Austin'); the day is not found and defaults to 01. The pool's chronology lens calls her 'formerly one of his philosophy students', which is wrong: she was a current Somerville undergraduate reading Greats. Coordinate corrected from 51.7627/-1.2649, about 420 m north of the college in the Radcliffe Observatory Quarter, to Wikipedia's 51.7592/-1.2625.
stops.campa: Austin marries Jean Coutts, twenty-two, an undergraduate reading Greats at Somerville, and the marriage makes her one of the first women Oxford permits to stay up while married. Somerville's redbrick quadrangles are plain beside the medieval stone of the men's colleges; it is one of a handful of women's colleges the university then allows at all. She is years away from the philosophy career she will build after his death. The ceremony is private, wedged between two intelligence postings. They will have four children.

stops.name: The Old War Office, Whitehall, MI14 and the order of battle
stops.date_confidence: the secondment to MI14 is attested to 1941 (Rowe, via WebSearch summary; EBSCO Research Starters); the month is inferred from the sequence of postings and the day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: Seconded to MI14, the German Army section of Military Intelligence, Austin works out of a basement in the War Office on Whitehall, assessing the order of battle of Rommel's Afrika Korps. Inside two months he produces the deduction that makes his name in the section: from fragments, that Germany is about to reinforce the Italians in North Africa. The material is wireless intercept, prisoner interrogation and captured paper, none of it complete and none of it addressed to him. He works it the way he works a text. He is promoted captain the following March.
suggested_refs: The Old War Office Building, Whitehall, home of MI14
sources: M. W. Rowe, J. L. Austin: Philosopher and D-Day Intelligence Officer (OUP, 2023)

stops.name: London, the Advanced Intelligence Section and the name Martians
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested (Nagel, LRB). The section's exact London address is not documented and the pin is central London. Figure corrected: the pool's chronology lens says the unit grew to 'nearly five hundred'; Nagel gives a range of between three hundred and five hundred, from an original six or seven.
stops.campa: Austin is promoted captain and made head of the Advanced Intelligence Section of General Headquarters. Under him it grows from six or seven men to somewhere between three hundred and five hundred. He leaves the single-focus work of MI14 for something nearer command: organising other people's inferences into one picture a general can act on without reading a raw report. The section assembles an enemy's intentions out of wireless intercepts, aerial photographs and captured paper, and for the detachment of it the rest of GHQ calls them the Martians.
stops.quote: The trouble with you senior officers is always the same. It is not that you will try to run before you can walk. You will try to walk before you can stand.
stops.quote_source: Austin to a senior officer, quoted in M. W. Rowe, J. L. Austin: Philosopher and D-Day Intelligence Officer (OUP, 2023), cited in Thomas Nagel, 'Leader of the Martians', London Review of Books vol. 45 no. 17
suggested_refs: The Advanced Intelligence Section, GHQ, known as the Martians, 1942-1945
sources: Thomas Nagel, 'Leader of the Martians', London Review of Books vol. 45 no. 17

stops.name: Norfolk House, St James's Square, the coast read from paper
stops.date_confidence: the section's Norfolk House period runs through 1943 into early 1944 (Nagel, LRB; EBSCO); no month attested, defaulted to 01. Anachronism corrected: the pool put SHAEF at Norfolk House in 1943, but the building housed COSSAC that year and SHAEF was not constituted until mid-January 1944.
stops.campa: Through 1943 Austin's section works out of Norfolk House on St James's Square, where Eisenhower had planned Operation Torch the year before and where COSSAC now assembles the picture of the coast the Allies mean to invade. Austin oversees the collation of coastal defence intelligence for Normandy: beach gradients, the load-bearing capacity of sand, reefs, gun positions, the German units behind them. None of the product carries his name on it. His section is cleared for Ultra, the decrypt traffic coming out of Bletchley Park, where Alan Turing's machinery is breaking the naval cipher.
stops.quote: the most complete overview of the entire intelligence picture
stops.quote_source: Description of Austin's section, quoted in Thomas Nagel, 'Leader of the Martians', London Review of Books vol. 45 no. 17, drawing on M. W. Rowe's biography

stops.name: Camp Griffiss, Bushy Park, the last assessments before the invasion
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested for the SHAEF move (The D-Day Story, Portsmouth; The Royal Parks, 'Setting up Camp Griffiss Bushy Park'); the day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: SHAEF moves out of Norfolk House to Camp Griffiss, a hutted and tented headquarters put up inside a royal deer park west of London, and Austin's section moves with it. Eisenhower works from here in the weeks before the sixth of June, and Austin's section produces its final estimate of German dispositions in Normandy from this park. Intelligence officers run the largest order-of-battle operation of the war out of prefabricated huts under old chestnut trees, deer grazing the open ground between them.

stops.name: Omaha Beach, the regiment his section did not find
stops.date_confidence: attested (Nagel, LRB). Austin is in England on this date; the stop pins the intelligence product, not the man. The reference volumes his section produced are in the hands of the officers going ashore.
stops.campa: The reference volumes his section compiled are in the hands of officers going ashore along fifty miles of Normandy coast, and on the western sector they are wrong. The German 916th Grenadier Regiment is holding the bluffs above the beach the Americans call Omaha, and the Martians have not placed it there. Austin is in England. The casualty figure on that stretch of sand comes out of the same method as everything he is decorated for: an inference from fragments, made at a desk. Whether the regiment could have been found in the material his section held, or whether it was never in the material, the published record does not settle.
suggested_refs: The Overlord beach intelligence volumes issued to invading officers

stops.name: Bayeux, walking the ground the estimates described
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Nagel states that Austin followed Eisenhower's headquarters into France; no source consulted names the forward site or the date of crossing. Bayeux stands as a proxy for SHAEF's forward area and the month is inferred.
stops.campa: In the weeks after the landings Austin crosses the Channel with SHAEF's forward echelon as it sets up on French soil near Bayeux, the first city liberated intact. The record does not fix the village where his section pitched. He is by now a lieutenant colonel, and the officer who read the German order of battle for three years off a desk in London walks the country his estimates described: the bocage, hedge banks higher than a man, which held the advance for weeks longer than any planner had allowed for.
suggested_refs: SHAEF forward headquarters in Normandy, summer 1944
sources: Thomas Nagel, 'Leader of the Martians', London Review of Books vol. 45 no. 17

stops.name: The Low Countries, Arnhem and the Ardennes
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The pool gives only 'Continental Europe' with a regional centroid for Austin's 1944-45 campaign work; the coordinate is that centroid and not a documented posting. Arnhem falls in September 1944 and the Ardennes offensive runs December 1944 into January 1945; the stop is dated to the end of that sequence.
stops.campa: Austin's intelligence work runs on through the failure at Arnhem in September and the German counterattack through the Ardennes in December, the two occasions in the western campaign when the picture assembled from intercepts and aerial photographs failed the men holding the line. The Ardennes fighting runs on into January 1945. He tells his wife nothing about any of it, then or afterwards. He leaves the army in 1945 a lieutenant colonel, with the OBE, the French Croix de Guerre and the American Legion of Merit.
suggested_refs: Austin's OBE, Croix de Guerre and Officer of the Legion of Merit citations, 1945
sources: Thomas Nagel, 'Leader of the Martians', London Review of Books vol. 45 no. 17

stops.name: Magdalen College, Oxford, the return in October
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested (Nagel, LRB); the day defaults to 01. Coordinate reconciled with the corrected Magdalen pin at 51.7524/-1.2471.
stops.campa: Austin comes back to Magdalen and to philosophy tutorials six years and a world war after he last held one. Colleagues describe a changed manner: more commanding, far less patient with a loose argument, than the young don who left. Oxford philosophy in 1945 is still mostly logical positivism with idealist leftovers underneath it, and he sets about both with the attention he had been giving intercepted German. Gilbert Ryle, not a timid man, leaves the plainest account of what it was like to be in a room with him.
stops.quote: We were all frightened of him.
stops.quote_source: Gilbert Ryle on Austin, quoted in Thomas Nagel, 'Leader of the Martians', London Review of Books vol. 45 no. 17 (2023)

stops.name: Manchester, Other Minds at the Joint Session
stops.date_confidence: attested to July 1946 (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; Aristotelian Society Supplementary Volume 20, pp. 148-187); the day is not recorded and defaults to 01. Place corrected: the pool put the paper in London, but the 1946 Joint Session was held at Manchester.
stops.campa: Austin reads 'Other Minds' to the Joint Session of the Aristotelian Society and the Mind Association at Manchester, in symposium with John Wisdom and A. J. Ayer. It is the first full statement of the method. Instead of asking how anyone can know that another mind exists, he asks what a person is doing when they say 'I know', and finds the answer sits closer to promising than to reporting an inner state. The symposium runs to forty pages of the Society's supplementary volume.
suggested_refs: J. L. Austin, 'Other Minds', Proceedings of the Aristotelian Society, Supplementary Volume 20 (1946), pp. 148-187
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'John Langshaw Austin'

stops.name: All Souls College, Oxford, the Saturday Mornings begin
stops.date_confidence: 1947 per EBSCO Research Starters, which states that Austin brought the dons together that year. The pool's chronology lens dates the group to 1953, six years later; the discrepancy is recorded here and the earlier date taken, since it is the one carrying a source that describes the founding. The meeting rooms are not fixed anywhere and All Souls stands as the representative Oxford venue.
stops.campa: Austin convenes a weekly gathering of younger Oxford philosophers to work through one text or one problem in unhurried detail, sometimes a whole term on a single question. Attendance is by invitation and the tone is unsparing: he chairs rather than lectures, cuts off tangents, and holds the group to the sentence actually in front of it. Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics and Frege's Grundlagen both go under the knife this way. Grice, Strawson, Hart and Warnock all pass through it. It runs in term time for over a decade.
stops.quote: what philosophy is so often thought, and made, barren of, the fun of discovery, the pleasures of co-operation, and the satisfaction of reaching agreement
stops.quote_source: J. L. Austin on collaborative method, quoted in Thomas Nagel, 'Leader of the Martians', London Review of Books vol. 45 no. 17 (2023)
suggested_refs: The Saturday Mornings group, Oxford, 1947 to 1959

stops.name: Broad Street, Oxford, Frege put into English
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Wikipedia; Journal of Symbolic Logic review records). Publisher corrected: the pool's geography lens gave Clarendon Press on Walton Street, but the 1950 translation was published by Basil Blackwell of Oxford, with Philosophical Library, New York, for the American edition. stops.campa: Basil Blackwell publishes Austin's translation of Frege's Die Grundlagen der Arithmetik as The Foundations of Arithmetic, German and English on facing pages, sixteen shillings; the American edition goes to Philosophical Library in New York. Frege had been close to unreadable in English before it. The work is slow and exact, a German logician's argument about what a number is put into English a philosopher can read at speed. Frege's complaint throughout the book is that the surface grammar of a sentence misleads you about what the sentence is doing.

stops.date_confidence: year attested (Britannica; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; Wikipedia); month and day default to 01. The pool's two lenses give Corpus Christi coordinates about sixty metres apart, 51.7508/-1.2531 and 51.7513/-1.2536; the second is taken and the discrepancy recorded.
stops.campa: Austin is elected to White's Chair of Moral Philosophy, Oxford's senior post in the subject, with the professorial fellowship attached to Corpus Christi, a small college wedged between Merton and Christ Church around a pillar sundial. He is forty-one, and will hold the chair until his death eight years later. It carries a platform and no obligation to use it gently, and it puts him at the head of the subject in a university that is by now the centre of ordinary language philosophy in English.

stops.name: Oxford, the course called Words and Deeds
stops.date_confidence: Urmson's preface to How to Do Things with Words gives the course as delivered in each of the years 1952 to 1954; the pool's geography lens gives 1951 to 1954, which is a year early at the front. The lecture room is not documented anywhere consulted, and the pool's assignment of it to the Examination Schools is unsupported, so the pin is the city.
stops.campa: Austin gives a lecture course, titled at various points 'Words and Deeds,' in which he first separates constative utterances, which describe the world and can be true or false, from performative utterances, which describe nothing and perform an action simply by being said. I do. I name this ship. I bet you sixpence it will rain tomorrow. The course exists only as notes, revised in each of the three years he gives it, and its last Oxford outing is in 1954. Nothing of it is published in his lifetime.
stops.quote: They do not 'describe' or 'report' or constate anything at all, are not 'true or false'
stops.quote_source: J. L. Austin, How to Do Things with Words, Lecture I (from the 1955 William James Lectures; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1962)

stops.name: Harvard University, the William James Lectures open
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to venue and month. The year 1955 and the count of twelve lectures are attested (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; Oxford Academic; Urmson's preface), but no source consulted names the hall or the month. Emerson Hall is inferred from the Harvard philosophy department's address since 1905, and the coordinate is corrected from the pool's 42.3736/-71.119, about 200 m southwest of the building.
stops.campa: Austin crosses the Atlantic to deliver the William James Lectures, twelve of them, without a finished manuscript. He opens against what he names the descriptive fallacy, the assumption that a sentence's only business is to state a fact truly or falsely. Against it he sets a class of sentences that do something merely by being uttered in the right circumstances by the right person, and calls them performatives. He warns the room at once that no grammatical test will sort them cleanly from ordinary statements. There is no book behind any of this; he is working from notes already revised through three Oxford deliveries.
stops.quote: I name this ship the Queen Elizabeth.
stops.quote_source: J. L. Austin, How to Do Things with Words, Lecture I
suggested_refs: Emerson Hall, Harvard, home of the philosophy department since 1905

sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'John Langshaw Austin'

stops.name: Harvard University, misfires and abuses
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The content is Lecture II and is well attested; the month is not. The pool carried March 1955 as though documented, but only the year of the series is fixed anywhere consulted, and the months here are ordering devices, not dates.
stops.campa: In the second lecture Austin turns from what performatives are to the ways they go wrong. A performative is never true or false, but it can misfire, when the speaker lacks the authority or the situation lacks the convention: an unlicensed bystander says 'I now pronounce you man and wife' and nobody is thereby married. Or it can be an abuse, correctly staged and hollow, as in a promise made with no intention of keeping it. He sets out the conditions a happy performative has to meet. Nobody, he notes, can baptise a penguin with a bottle of beer.
suggested_refs: J. L. Austin, How to Do Things with Words, Lecture II, on felicity conditions
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'John Langshaw Austin'

stops.name: Harvard Yard, the meeting with Chomsky
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The meeting is attested only as a bare fact (Wikipedia, 'J. L. Austin'), with no date and no location within the campus. Harvard Yard is a representative pin and the month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Somewhere in the walks and dinners a visiting lecturer's schedule generates, Austin meets Noam Chomsky, then still years from Syntactic Structures. Nothing survives of what passed between them beyond the fact that it happened. The two men are two roads out of one problem, without either fully knowing it yet: one running toward a generative grammar indifferent to who speaks and when, the other toward what a sentence does when this person says it to that one in a given room.

stops.name: Harvard University, the distinction collapses
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to month; only the year of the series is documented anywhere consulted, and the month here orders the sequence rather than dating it. Lecture numbering corrected: the locutionary, illocutionary and perlocutionary trichotomy is introduced in Lecture VIII and elaborated in IX and X, and the collapse of the performative and constative distinction into the general doctrine of illocutionary force runs through Lectures XI and XII, where the classification into verdictives, exercitives, commissives, behabitives and expositives is given.
stops.campa: By the closing lectures Austin abandons the split he spent the first half building. Performative against constative will not hold, he argues, because his own examples keep crossing it. In its place he puts a three-part analysis of every utterance whatever: the locutionary act, saying something with a sense and a reference; the illocutionary act, what is done in saying it, promising, warning, naming, asking; and the perlocutionary act, what is brought about by saying it, persuading, alarming, convincing. Even a plain statement of fact performs one. Stating is an act.
stops.quote: Is it not possible that the next century may see the birth, through the joint labours of philosophers, grammarians and numerous other students of language, of a true and comprehensive science of language?
stops.quote_source: J. L. Austin, quoted in Thomas Nagel, 'Leader of the Martians', London Review of Books vol. 45 no. 17 (2023)
suggested_refs: J. L. Austin, How to Do Things with Words, Lectures VIII to XII

The full sentence behind the closing clause, at p. 139 of the 1962 edition: 'Once we realize that what we have to study is not the sentence but the issuing of an utterance in a speech situation, there can hardly be any longer a possibility of not seeing that stating is performing an act.'

J. L. Austin, How to Do Things with Words (1962)

segments.name: The Formula That Does Not Describe: Magic and Prophecy

stops.name: Oxford, the spell as the purest performative
stops.date_confidence: interpretive. The stop applies Austin's own published categories (How to Do Things with Words, Lectures I-II) to a class of utterance, the magical formula, that Austin himself never names in any source consulted. The scholarly bridge is later and is not his: S. J. Tambiah's Malinowski Memorial Lecture of 1968 is the first cited work to read ritual spell-language through Austin's illocutionary framework. The date is placed just after the Harvard lectures close as an ordering device and is not attested to any documented act of Austin's.
stops.campa: Austin's own examples are civic: a ship named, a bet laid, a couple pronounced married. The class he defines reaches further back than any registry office. A curse spoken over a cradle, a name spoken to bind a spirit, a word said to open a locked door: none of them describes a state of affairs already there. Each, said by the right mouth under the right conditions, brings it about. The formula does not report the curse; the formula is the curse. A constative answers to the world, true or false against it. The spell answers to nothing but its felicity conditions. Get them wrong, an unlicensed voice, a missing ingredient, and it misfires.
stops.quote: To utter the sentence (in, of course, the appropriate circumstances) is not to describe my doing of what I should be said in so uttering to be doing or to state that I am doing it: it is to do it.
stops.quote_source: J. L. Austin, How to Do Things with Words (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1962), Lecture I
suggested_refs: J. L. Austin, How to Do Things with Words, Lectures I-II, on the performative and its felicity conditions

S. J. Tambiah, 'The Magical Power of Words', Man n.s. 3 (1968), the Malinowski Memorial Lecture that reads ritual spell-language as Austinian performative, and his 1979 Radcliffe-Brown Lecture on the imperative transfer
sources: J. L. Austin, How to Do Things with Words (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1962), Lectures I-II
S. J. Tambiah, 'The Magical Power of Words', Man, New Series, vol. 3 no. 2 (1968), pp. 175-208

stops.name: Briar Rose, the fated word: prophecy as performative
stops.date_confidence: interpretive. The stop applies Austin's performative and felicity framework to the fairy tale as a test case; Austin himself is not on record discussing Briar Rose, Sleeping Beauty, or fairy-tale material in any source consulted. The primary texts for the curse are attested: 'Dornroschen', Kinder- und Hausmarchen (1812, rev. 1857), tale no. 50, quoted here in Margaret Hunt's 1884 translation, and Perrault's 'La Belle au bois dormant' (1697). The Kinder- und Hausmarchen occasion is a feast for the birth, not a christening; the christening detail belongs to Perrault, and a widely repeated conflation of the two is corrected here. The speakers are wise women in the German text and fairies in the French. The date is an ordering device only.
stops.campa: A prophecy is ordinarily read as a prediction, a sentence checked later against the fact, true or false the way a constative is. Austin's frame reads it otherwise: the saying is not a bet placed on the future but an act performed upon it. At the feast for the newborn princess twelve wise women give their gifts, and a thirteenth, left off the list because the king owns only twelve golden plates, comes in unbidden, speaks last, and speaks over the cradle. The words are a bare declarative in the future tense. Nobody in the tale takes them for a forecast that might turn out to have been wrong.
stops.quote: The King's daughter shall in her fifteenth year prick herself with a spindle, and fall down dead.
stops.quote_source: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, 'Little Briar-Rose', Kinder- und Hausmarchen, tale no. 50, trans. Margaret Hunt, Grimm's Household Tales (1884)
suggested_refs: 'Dornroschen', Kinder- und Hausmarchen (1812, rev. 1857), tale no. 50
Charles Perrault, 'La Belle au bois dormant', Histoires ou contes du temps passe (1697), where the occasion is a christening and the speakers are fairies

stops.name: Briar Rose, the amendment and the burned spindles
stops.date_confidence: interpretive, and dated only to order the segment. The tale's sequence is attested in the Kinder- und Hausmarchen (Hunt's 1884 translation): the twelfth wise woman speaks after the curse and softens it, the king orders the spindles burnt, the girl finds a spindle at fifteen. Perrault's 1697 version differs in the detail: the young fairy who mitigates is one of the seven invited godmothers, who has hidden herself behind the hangings in order to speak last, and no one is summoned from afar, a point often got wrong in retellings.
stops.campa: A twelfth speaker who has not yet given her wish cannot revoke what has been said. She can only amend it, and death becomes a hundred years' sleep. The king then orders every spindle in the kingdom burnt, a whole polity organizing itself around foreclosing the conditions of one uttered clause. At fifteen the girl finds the spindle the decree missed, in a tower room, in an old woman's hands.
stops.quote: It shall not be death, but a deep sleep of a hundred years, into which the king's daughter shall fall.
stops.quote_source: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, 'Little Briar-Rose', Kinder- und Hausmarchen, tale no. 50, trans. Margaret Hunt, Grimm's Household Tales (1884)
suggested_refs: 'Dornroschen', Kinder- und Hausmarchen (1812, rev. 1857), tale no. 50

stops.name: Oxford, Ifs and Cans
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; Proceedings of the British Academy); month and day default to 01. The pin is the city, since the paper is a publication rather than an event with a room.
stops.campa: Austin publishes 'Ifs and Cans' in the Proceedings of the British Academy. The paper works on two of the smallest words in English, the ones philosophers writing about freedom and action reach for without looking: what a man can do, and what he could have done if he had chosen. It is a short paper about a conditional, and it is one of the very few things Austin lets into print at all. He is forty-five, and most of his work is spoken, in rooms, to people who take notes and publish under their own names later.

stops.name: London, the presidential address to the Aristotelian Society
stops.date_confidence: delivered at the opening of the 1956-57 session and printed as Proceedings of the Aristotelian Society vol. 57, pp. 1-30. The pool's chronology lens dates the delivery to 1957, a year late; the geography lens has 1956 and is followed here. Senate House as the venue is not documented for that year, only that the Society continues to meet there, so the pin is a reconstruction rather than an attestation. The day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: As president of the Aristotelian Society Austin delivers 'A Plea for Excuses' at the opening of the session. The paper argues that the vocabulary people actually use to excuse, justify and explain what they have done carries more distinctions than any invented technical language a philosopher could put in its place, and that this vocabulary is therefore where the work should start. He picks excuses because they are unglamorous, and because an action shows its joints where it has gone wrong. The address runs to thirty pages of the Society's Proceedings.
stops.quote: our common stock of words embodies all the distinctions men have found worth drawing, and the connexions they have found worth marking, in the lifetimes of many generations of men
stops.quote_source: J. L. Austin, 'A Plea for Excuses: The Presidential Address', Proceedings of the Aristotelian Society vol. 57 (1956-57), pp. 1-30

stops.name: Berkeley, the case against sense-data
stops.date_confidence: autumn 1958 attested (Wikipedia, 'J. L. Austin'); the pool's chronology lens dates the American visits to the mid-1950s and pins 1958 to Berkeley, and both stand. The specific lecture building is not documented; Wheeler Hall is a representative Berkeley venue and the coordinate is that building. The day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: Austin lectures at the University of California through the autumn, giving both the seminar on excuses and the material published after his death as Sense and Sensibilia: a demolition of the sense-datum, the private intermediate object philosophers had inserted between a perceiver and the world. He works here as he always works, from notes and out loud. Against Ayer, Price and Warnock alike he insists that ordinary perceptual talk already draws distinctions the sense-datum vocabulary flattens out, and that the philosophers' examples of illusion have been chosen to make the case they were wanted for.
stops.quote: There is no one kind of thing that we 'perceive' but many different kinds.
stops.quote_source: J. L. Austin, Sense and Sensibilia (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1962)

stops.name: Oxford, taken ill on the road back from Scandinavia
stops.date_confidence: early October 1959 per Rowe's chapter 'Final Illness: 1959-1960', which has Austin falling ill on the return from Scandinavia with tests showing lung cancer soon after. The pool's chronology and geography lenses both date the diagnosis to December 1959, two months late; the earlier date is taken and the discrepancy recorded. The day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: Austin falls ill on the way back from Scandinavia in the first days of October. The tests come back quickly and show lung cancer, already advanced. He is forty-eight, still White's Professor, and he has four months left. He works through nearly all of them. The Harvard lectures are still a bundle of notes and the perception lectures are still a bundle of notes, five years and four deliveries after he first gave either of them. Whether he meant to make books of them, or meant them to stay talk, the record of this autumn does not say.

stops.name: Churchill Hospital, Oxford, the radiation
stops.date_confidence: treatment at the Churchill attested by Rowe; the month is inferred from the sequence in his 'Final Illness' chapter and the day defaults to 01. The pool's geography lens placed this episode at the Radcliffe Infirmary as an inference from period Oxford medical geography; that inference is superseded by the source. Two coordinates for the Churchill appear in the pool, 51.7434/-1.2065 and 51.7423/-1.2076, about 130 m apart; the second is taken.
stops.campa: He is treated with radiation at the Churchill Hospital on the eastern edge of Oxford, a wartime hutted hospital the city kept after the American medical corps built it. By Christmas he is very ill. By the middle of January he is dying. His wife still does not know what he did between 1940 and 1945. The name of his unit, the beaches, the volumes he compiled, the citation for the Legion of Merit: none of it is discussed in the house, and he does not use the months to tell her.

stops.name: Oxford, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; Nagel, LRB). The pool's geography lens says he died 'seven weeks after his diagnosis', which does not survive the corrected October date; four months is the correct interval.
stops.campa: Austin dies on the eighth of February 1960, aged forty-eight, four months after the diagnosis. He leaves How to Do Things with Words as a bundle of lecture notes revised over a decade and delivered four times, three at Oxford and once at Harvard, never set down as a text he considered finished. Sense and Sensibilia is in the same condition. Warnock and Urmson, his colleagues and former pupils, will spend two years reconstructing both. The obituaries call him the most influential philosopher in Oxford of his generation.

stops.name: Magdalen College, Oxford, a death marked and a grave unrecorded
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Oxford's marking of the death is general in the sources and no memorial service, chapel, or hall is named anywhere consulted. No grave, cremation record, burial register entry, or Find a Grave memorial was located for Austin. The date is placed a week after the death purely to order the stop and is not attested.
stops.campa: Oxford marks the death at Magdalen, the college he taught in from 1935 until the war took him, and where he kept rooms and friendships afterwards even once the chair moved his formal fellowship to Corpus Christi. Men who had sat through the Saturday Mornings and men who had served under him in the section both attend. Where he was buried, or whether he was buried at all, no source consulted will say. Dons of his generation commonly lie at Wolvercote. Nothing found puts Austin among them.

segments.name: The Books Made Out of the Notes

stops.name: Clarendon Press, Oxford, Philosophical Papers
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; Clarendon Press catalogue records); month and day default to 01. The pool's two lenses give Walton Street coordinates about 130 m apart, 51.7583/-1.2648 and 51.7594/-1.2621; the second is taken.
stops.campa: Urmson and Warnock gather the essays into a single volume: 'Other Minds,' 'Ifs and Cans,' 'A Plea for Excuses,' 'The Meaning of a Word,' and the rest of what Austin had let into print or read aloud to societies over twenty-five years. Both editors are colleagues and former pupils of his, and Warnock had sat through the Saturday Mornings for years. It is the first time the method can be seen whole by anyone who was never in a room with him. It is also thin. Twenty-five years of work, collected, comes to one book of moderate length.

stops.name: Clarendon Press, Oxford, How to Do Things with Words
stops.date_confidence: year attested; published simultaneously by Clarendon Press, Oxford and Harvard University Press (Cambridge and Oxford Academic publication records). Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: Urmson edits the Harvard notes into a book, published on the same day by Clarendon Press in Oxford and by Harvard University Press, two years after Austin's death and seven years after the lectures. The performative and constative distinction is abandoned inside it exactly as it was abandoned in the room, and what survives is the general theory of illocutionary force, with its misfires and its abuses, its unhappy rather than its false. The opening sentence comes through the editing untouched.
stops.quote: What I shall have to say here is neither difficult nor contentious; the only merit I should like to claim for it is that of being true, at least in parts.
stops.quote_source: J. L. Austin, How to Do Things with Words (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1962), Lecture I

stops.name: Clarendon Press, Oxford, Sense and Sensibilia
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; Clarendon Press records); the month is an ordering device to separate this volume from How to Do Things with Words in the same year, and the day defaults to 01. The title's pun on Jane Austen is standard in the literature but is not documented in the verified pool and is carried as reconstruction.
stops.campa: Warnock reconstructs the perception lectures from Austin's manuscript notes and publishes them under the punning title Austin himself had given the course. The book is a demolition and nothing else: it builds no theory of perception to replace the one it takes apart. Its method is to work through the examples philosophers reach for, the mirage and the stick that looks bent in water, and to show that ordinary language had them sorted into kinds before any theory arrived to flatten them. Austin had been dead two years when it appeared, and the arrangement of the chapters is Warnock's.
stops.quote: Usually it is uses of words, not words in themselves, that are properly called 'vague.'
stops.quote_source: J. L. Austin, Sense and Sensibilia (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1962), p. 126

stops.name: Harvard University Press, Cambridge, the corrected second edition
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Harvard University Press listing; Cambridge University Press publication record); month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: Urmson and Marina Sbisa go back to Austin's original papers and re-edit the book, reconciling manuscript variants the first edition had smoothed over and adding an appendix of his marginal notes. Thirteen years after the first edition and twenty after the lectures, the text is still being assembled out of the paper of a man who never wrote it. Speech act theory is by this point in linguistics, in law and in literary criticism, and Derrida's essay asking whether a performative survives being quoted has been in print three years, with Searle's reply still to come.
